member_of.name: Blue Rodeo (Greg Keelor - not a band member but strong connection)

podcast.title: Band Longevity and Lineup Stability (1980-Present)
podcast.body: 5440 has been active since 1980. Despite a few lineup changes (three by one account), the core members have remained with the group, demonstrating remarkable stability and dedication over four decades. "This band has been a going concern since 1980. And well, there have been a couple of lineup changes over the years, three by my account. The core of the group is still there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Existential Moment: Dropped by Warner (c. 1995)
podcast.body: After the release of their sixth album, "Smiling Buddha Cabaret," the band was dropped by their American label, Warner. This presented an "existential moment" where they considered quitting but ultimately decided to continue on their own terms rather than following external pressures. "Another existential moment. Another moment where you could pack it in or decide you're going to go on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Transition Period and Songwriting Volume (c. 1995-1997)
podcast.body: During the period after being dropped by Warner and before signing with Sony Music Canada, the band entered a "couple of years" of transition, actively writing a large volume of songs. For a potential record (referred to as "dear, dear record"), they had accumulated approximately 30 to 40 songs. "Drew, we must have had 30 or 40 songs. We have about 30 songs for the dear, dear record."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Raine Maida's Intervention in Labatt's Standoff (c. 1997)
podcast.body: During a standoff at a festival in Manitoba (part of the "Trusted by Millions" tour, around 1997-1998) over a Labatt's balloon on stage, Raine Maida, the singer from Our Lady Peace, intervened. He explained 5440's contractual clauses to the promoters, resulting in the balloon being deflated, allowing 5440 to perform. "thanks to him, they took it down."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Securing a Deal with Sony Music Canada (c. 1997)
podcast.body: Sony Music Canada, under the leadership of Paul Berger and A&R representative Richard Zuckerman, became interested in 5440 as it sought to grow. This led to a new record deal for the band, though without an accompanying American contract. "Paul Berger was brought in to run the company. And he was eager to find stuff. And somebody mentioned us to him and Richard Zuckerman, who was his A&R guy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Anti-Commercial Stance (Pre-1998)
podcast.body: Initially, 5440 was strongly against commercial endorsements, embodying a "nearly young don't sing for Miller don't sing for Bud kind of vibe." They turned down offers from cigarette companies and had contractual control over stage visibility, once refusing to play a festival opening for Pearl Jam until a Labatt's balloon was deflated, leading to a standoff. "we were totally against that... cigarette companies... nearly young don't sing for Miller don't sing for Bud kind of vibe."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shift to Accepting Commercial Licensing (Post-1998)
podcast.body: The band's stance on licensing evolved, particularly after signing with Sony, which offered publishing deals that provided upfront money for things like house down payments. They also recognized that pop songs in commercials were becoming a primary driver of song discovery, similar to what TikTok does today, making it a "new reality." "at that time, songs, pop songs on commercials, we're driving, it's kind of like what TikTok is doing now. People were re-discovering hit songs and stuff like that and you just sort of had to accept once again, that's what that's the new reality."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "I Go Blind" on the Friends Soundtrack
podcast.body: The 5440 song "I Go Blind" was included on the soundtrack for the TV show "Friends." This came about because the A&R executive assembling the soundtrack was the same person who had signed Hootie & the Blowfish to their label. Hootie had recorded "I Go Blind" but cut it from their first album, allowing its use on the soundtrack with the stipulation that it not be released as a single. "It ends up with a friend soundtrack, right?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ambivalence Towards Publishing Deals
podcast.body: The band describes publishing deals as a "double-edged sword." While they provide upfront money (e.g., down payments for houses), musicians later realize they are giving away rights to half their future income after the initial recoupment. "you sell the rights to half of your songs... Wait a minute. I'm giving you half of all my money now. So it's double edged sword there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: COVID-19 as an Impetus for New Music
podcast.body: During the COVID-19 pandemic, Brad Merritt initiated Zoom calls with the band members, who live in different locations (three on islands, Dave in Vancouver). These calls, initially for reminiscing and telling stories, became the creative spark for their upcoming album, "West Coast Band," where stories from their history are transformed into songs. "Brad came up with the idea of, you know, doing a Zoom call. So we got them and this is this became the impetus, which is for the record that's going to come out next, because we just started telling stories."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Changing Radio/TV Support (Mid-2000s)
podcast.body: The band experienced a shift in support from Canadian music channels like MuchMusic, being told they were being moved to outlets like "MuchLOUD" or other less prominent channels. This indicated that their generation of bands was being phased out of mainstream "cool" rotation. "you get told like, yeah, much music isn't going to play. They're throwing you over too much light or whatever the hell it was called."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collaboration with Garth Richardson
podcast.body: Garth Richardson worked on projects with 5440. "That led to more work with everyone from Motley Crew to 5440 and Kitty and Mudvane and Chavelle and the Catherine Wheel and Trapped."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Commercial Licensing of "Since When" Song
podcast.body: The song "Since When" was licensed for TV commercials, including campaigns for Telus and High on Day. This licensing helped the band to recoup their Sony publishing deal, highlighting a new revenue stream in a changing music landscape. "that song, because it was a tell us and a high on day commercial and some other thing and we recouped all of our Sony publishing publishing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: David Gen Collaboration
podcast.body: David Gen, who co-wrote the song "Make the Leave" for Ian Thorneley's "Tiny Pictures" album, also worked with the band 5440.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Decision for Artistic Autonomy
podcast.body: Following a negative experience with their "Show Me" record, which they felt was too influenced by the record company's path of least resistance, the band resolved to "stick together as a band" and pursue their "own thing," rather than solely listening to external advice. "So I think, well, we're just going to stick together as a band and not listen to these people anymore."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Digital Revolution and Industry Warnings (Early 2000s)
podcast.body: During the production of the "Casual Viewing" album, Sony Music Canada president Rick Kamillary warned Neil Osborne that the traditional music industry was "over" due to digital changes like Napster, with CDs "giving away masters" and record companies seeking an "exit plan." This foreshadowed the dramatic shift in music consumption. "He goes, it's over, Neil, it's all over... We're giving away masters, CDs is giving away masters and then Napster and all that started to happen. He goes, I'm looking for my ex a plan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dual Genre Identity: Classic vs. Modern Rock (Pre-COVID)
podcast.body: Just before the COVID-19 pandemic, 5440 experienced a weekend where they played two distinct festivals. On one day, they were the "youngest band on the bill" playing alongside classic rock acts like Boston and REO Speedwagon, effectively "graduating to classic rock." The very next day, they occupied a middle slot with younger, "super cool bands" like Wintersleep, realizing they were simultaneously embraced by "both camps." "We played two different festivals... So when we were we were a band new band in a classic rock we played with Boston and our EO speed wagon... and then the next day we were sort of in the middle slot of With winter sleep and all these I don't even know the names of these bands the super cool bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Encounter with an Aggressive Fan in St. Catharines
podcast.body: During a show in St. Catharines, an intoxicated woman managed to get into the dressing room. She became increasingly annoying and aggressive, eventually getting into an altercation with a bouncer, breaking his nose. It took three bouncers to remove her from the premises. "We did a show in St. Catherine's whereas it was a woman who worked her way into the dressing room and You know started to be really annoying and you know sit on my lap and I like you and all that and then I sort of Indicated to the bouncer like can you get rid of her please? And so he tried and she went off and hauled and broke his nose And she was tough So it took three bouncer's to get her out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolving Perspective on Longevity
podcast.body: Neil Osborne recounts his changing feelings about the band's duration as he aged, from dreading still being in the band at 30 and 40, to embracing it as "amazing" at 50, and expressing gratitude at 60 for the opportunity to continue. "I'm 30 now shoot myself... I'm 40 shoot me... I'm 50. Amen. This is amazing. And now I'm 60. And it's like, oh my God, I can't believe I get to do this."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Existential Conversation: Adapting to the Digital Age (2000s)
podcast.body: Facing the decline of the traditional music business and seeing friends lose record deals, Neil Osborne and Brad Merritt had an "existential conversation" at Nathan Phillips Square in Toronto. They decided to leverage their existing body of work from the "old system" while learning to navigate and adapt to the emerging "digital world." "because that was another point where we were saying, yeah, we could just pack it in now and find something else to do. Or how are we going to sort of move forward?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Garth Richardson's Production Style for "Since When"
podcast.body: Producer Garth Richardson, known for producing numerous platinum-selling "testosterone, big muscle tattoo, thick neck" records, adapted his approach for 5440's "Since When." The band specifically requested a 16-track, two-inch, intimate record with strings, a departure from his usual "beef records," which Richardson executed well. "Garth is an excellent producer and he went with it and you know, we had the song since when."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hootie & the Blowfish's Fandom and Cover of "I Go Blind"
podcast.body: Hootie & the Blowfish were early fans of 5440, having attended their shows at the 930 Club in Washington, DC, and covered nearly every song from 5440's "Green Record" in their own cover band, alongside R.E.M. songs. "they came up from University of South Carolina and they were fans. And they played almost every song off the Green Record in their cover band and every REM song that we were there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hootie & the Blowfish's Support for 5440
podcast.body: The members of Hootie & the Blowfish were very supportive of 5440 regarding the success of "I Go Blind." They invited 5440 to tour with them, and their drummer, Sony, personally showed them a Billboard chart indicating "I Go Blind" at number three on Hot AC, assuring them of incoming royalties. "The band were very, very happy for us. We did some tour with them... Sony was, came in with the billboard... he goes, you guys are going to get some money. You know, this is great. I make sure you get every penny."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Late 1980s Success
podcast.body: 5440 was among the new acts signed throughout the late 1980s who achieved hits and solid-selling albums. This success was incentivized by the serious prospect of radio airplay, coverage by MuchMusic, and funding assistance, reflecting a growing investment in Canadian talent by the recorded music industry. "Throughout the late 1980s, new acts were signed and had hits in solid-selling albums, Blue Rodeo, The Box, Pursuit of Happiness, Northern Pikes, National Velvet, Alana Miles, 5440, Cowboy Junkeys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of the 90s CanRock Explosion

podcast.title: Loss of Control Over Venue Branding
podcast.body: The band eventually lost the battle against corporate branding in venues. Molson, Bud, Labatt's, and cigarette companies began directly contracting with venues and promoters, making it impossible for bands to play without encountering corporate logos. This meant bands no longer had a choice in performing on a "Coca-Cola stage" or similar, losing the fight without realizing it. "the Moulson and the cigarette companies went directly to the venues, went directly to the promoters where if you wanted to play at all, you had to see Moulson or Bud or LaBaz or, you know, players light or whatever it was, or Coke, you didn't have a choice anymore."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Music Ownership Structure
podcast.body: 5440 owned all their publishing rights for songs created before their Sony deal. For songs recorded with Sony, Sony owned both the masters and the publishing rights, although the band was "paid handsomely" for these arrangements. "we had all of our publishing from before Sony... all the Sony publishing was owned by all the songs we recorded with Sony. They published... They own the masters. Yeah."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Music Video Production Frustrations (Late 1990s)
podcast.body: The band expressed frustration with the traditional music video production process, which involved large budgets (e.g., 200 grand) for what they perceived as uninspired concepts, often by trendy young directors, such as standing in a "cold, cold puddle in a warehouse." "We would do these videos for 200 grand and they'd hire some student out of Mexico City... I'm like, well, what the hell is this about? This is stupid."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Organic Radio Success of "I Go Blind" Cover
podcast.body: Despite Hootie & the Blowfish's request not to release "I Go Blind" as a single from the "Friends" soundtrack, radio stations in places like Boulder or Denver started playing it due to Hootie's immense popularity and its "anti-Nirvana" vibe. This led to organic fan requests and widespread airplay, effectively overriding Hootie's new official single. "Just picked just because Hoody was like all the rage, right? It was sort of the anti-Nurvana and people started requesting it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Philosophy of Continuous Creation
podcast.body: The band's guiding principle for longevity and success is to "just keep creating, keep writing" and to pursue what you love, trusting that "everything should take care of itself." "Just keep creating, keep writing. If you love it, do it. And then maybe something will happen. Maybe it won't, but at least you'll be doing what you love."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Revolutionary Mission and Influences (Early Career)
podcast.body: Singer Neil Osborne describes the band's early days as being "on a mission" to "change the world," viewing themselves as "revolutionaries" in the vein of bands like The Clash and U2. This reflects an early ethos driven by artistic and social ambition. "We were on a mission. We were going to change the world. We were like revolutionaries, you know, like the clash and sad and eats the and all that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rolling Stones Longevity Metric
podcast.body: Brad Merritt uses The Rolling Stones as a benchmark for 5440's own career length, stating that when The Rolling Stones quit, that would serve as 5440's "20 year warning," as 5440 started 20 years after the Stones. "when the rolling stones quit, that's our 20 year warning because we started 20 years after they started."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Touring Accident: Lane Guy Falls from Bus
podcast.body: During a tour stop at a Tower Records Convention in Sacramento, the band's "lane guy" (likely a sound or stage tech) accidentally missed a jump seat in the front of the bus. He hit the door handle on the way out and rolled out of the moving bus. Although not funny at the moment, he emerged unharmed, making it a memorable and eventually humorous road story. "He hits the door handling the way out and then rolls out the bus and we're literally you know 100 meters before we're able to stop So That was it wasn't funny at the moment, but when he rolled around got up and said I'm okay."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Trip to Moscow During Gorbachev Era
podcast.body: The band embarked on a week-long exchange trip to Moscow while Mikhail Gorbachev was still in power. They witnessed the last Communist May Day parade and performed a show with a local band called The Scramblers, who later got into trouble with authorities but were released after mentioning "Gretzky." "We were there for a week in an exchange thing while Gorbachev was still the head of It was we saw the last made a parade the last communist made a parade We did a show there with a band called the scramblers, you know who ended up getting in jail and stuff like that Once they said the word gretzky they got let out a jail."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Unexpected Royalties from "I Go Blind"
podcast.body: The significant financial success of Hootie & the Blowfish's cover of "I Go Blind" generated a substantial amount of "mailbox money" for 5440. The first royalty check was so large that Neil Osborne's wife initially believed it was a mistake due to the numerous zeros. "My wife calling me because she used to get the checks in the mail. They made a mistake. They made a mistake. We got to give it back... because there's so many zeros on that first check."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
